title: The Settlement With Gaps
briefing: The articles of the Religious Peace of Augsburg lie in every imperial dispute. Catholic and Lutheran estates are to be left in their lands, rites, jurisdictions, rents, and privileges; violence on account of confession is forbidden; those outside the two recognized confessions are excluded from the peace.
situation: Memorials before the court point to the same articles for opposite purposes. Catholic petitioners ask when alienated ecclesiastical lands and revenues will be restored. Lutheran estates answer that long possession, schools, churches, and local practice now stand under the peace. Each disputed monastery, parish, city, and mediate lordship waits for judgment.
historian_note: Wilson treats Augsburg as part of the Empire's constitutional settlement rather than a simple pause in religious war. Its unresolved legal-confessional questions became usable political weapons once rulers and estates ceased trusting one another's interpretation.

options.label: Assert the strict clauses of the settlement and prepare to close disputed usages.
options.consequence: Catholic petitioners leave court with stronger expectation that old rights will be heard. Lutheran and mixed estates begin preparing memorials of their own, warning that enforcement against settled practice will disturb the public peace it claims to defend.

options.label: Preserve Augsburg as a living compact, to be clarified only by consultation.
options.consequence: The court appears as guardian of the settlement rather than master of its ambiguities. Moderate estates remain at the table, while Catholic reformers complain that churches, revenues, and privileges are being withheld under the name of peace.

options.label: Let disputed usages stand until a concrete complaint forces judgment.
options.consequence: The files remain open and no estate is forced to retreat today. Local officers, consistories, chapters, and councils continue to gather proofs for the next quarrel.

title: Leagues of Protection
briefing: Reports arrive from Auhausen and Munich. Palatine councillors have sealed a Protestant Union, promising correspondence, mutual aid, transit, contributions, and defence of estates who claim the ordinary courts no longer protect them. Catholic ecclesiastical princes answer by binding themselves to a League under Maximilian of Bavaria.
situation: Both associations send assurances that they act for the public peace, not against the emperor. Their articles speak of counsel, compensation, lawful process, and assistance only in danger. Yet each letter also names commanders, treasuries, quotas, warnings, and the right to move when delay threatens land and people.
historian_note: Wilson stresses that the Union and Liga did not make war inevitable. They mattered because they turned insecurity into institutions and gave ambitious directors ways to spread costs, claim legitimacy, and mobilize support.

memory_variants.briefing: Because the court has chosen stricter enforcement of the Augsburg settlement, the reports from Auhausen and Munich arrive as warnings of organized resistance. Palatine councillors have sealed a Protestant Union, promising correspondence, mutual aid, transit, contributions, and defence of estates who claim the ordinary courts no longer protect them. Catholic ecclesiastical princes answer by binding themselves to a League under Maximilian of Bavaria.
memory_variants.situation: That earlier posture gives Catholic petitioners confidence that old rights may be pressed, but it also sharpens Protestant claims that ordinary remedies have become unsafe. Each association sends assurances that it acts for the public peace, not against the emperor; each also names commanders, treasuries, quotas, warnings, and the right to move when delay threatens land and people.

memory_variants.briefing: Because the court has chosen consultation over immediate enforcement, the reports from Auhausen and Munich arrive as warnings rather than summons. Palatine councillors have sealed a Protestant Union, promising correspondence, mutual aid, transit, contributions, and defence of estates who claim the ordinary courts no longer protect them. Catholic ecclesiastical princes answer by binding themselves to a League under Maximilian of Bavaria.
memory_variants.situation: The reports add that earlier posture gives Ferdinand a language of restraint, but it also makes both leagues harder to condemn at once. Each association sends assurances that it acts for the public peace, not against the emperor; each also names commanders, treasuries, quotas, warnings, and the right to move when delay threatens land and people.

memory_variants.briefing: Because the court has left disputed usages to stand until complaint forces judgment, the reports from Auhausen and Munich arrive beside a growing file of unanswered petitions. Palatine councillors have sealed a Protestant Union, promising correspondence, mutual aid, transit, contributions, and defence of estates who claim the ordinary courts no longer protect them. Catholic ecclesiastical princes answer by binding themselves to a League under Maximilian of Bavaria.
memory_variants.situation: That earlier posture avoids a single imperial provocation, but it leaves each estate to judge danger for itself. Each association sends assurances that it acts for the public peace, not against the emperor; each also names commanders, treasuries, quotas, warnings, and the right to move when delay threatens land and people.

options.label: Tolerate the leagues as temporary instruments, bound to imperial law.
options.consequence: The associations remain careful in their language and continue to profess obedience. Their members also keep their correspondence, treasuries, and pledges of aid, as if imperial justice may arrive too late.

options.label: Condemn the leagues as unlawful factions against the public peace.
options.consequence: The court speaks in the old language of the Landfrieden. Union and League members send replies insisting that their oaths were made for defence, and that delay by imperial institutions left their lands exposed.

options.label: Treat Catholic association as the necessary answer to Protestant coordination.
options.consequence: Catholic ecclesiastical princes send more confidently to Munich, and Bavarian direction becomes the obvious channel for armed Catholic aid. The emperor gains a shield, but one held in another prince's hand.

title: A Royal Promise in Bohemia
briefing: Copies of Rudolf's Letter of Majesty circulate through Prague and the provincial diets. Protestant estates point to its words when they speak of churches, schools, consistories, defenders, and the free exercise granted to them under royal seal.
situation: Royal councillors answer with distinctions over crown lands, ecclesiastical lordships, and the limits of the charter. The estates reply that a promise entered among the kingdom's liberties cannot be narrowed by officials without shaking the obedience owed to the crown.
historian_note: The Letter of Majesty makes the Bohemian crisis a dispute over recorded estate privileges as well as confession. Later enforcement could be presented as lawful correction by one side and charter-breaking by the other.

options.label: Uphold the Letter as a broad charter of Bohemian estate liberty.
options.consequence: The Protestant estates read the crown's answer as confirmation that obedience and chartered worship can stand together. Catholic councillors and clergy see a written barrier placed before restoration in one of the Habsburgs' principal kingdoms.

options.label: Read the Letter narrowly where royal and ecclesiastical rights are disputed.
options.consequence: Royal officials proceed with a defensible legal distinction. Protestant directors copy the same order into their grievance papers as proof that the charter is being emptied while its seal remains on display.

options.label: Avoid a formal ruling and leave local practice to bear the strain.
options.consequence: No order forces an immediate retreat. Parish officers, noble patrons, royal judges, and defenders continue to act under rival readings of the same royal paper.

title: The Styrian Lesson
briefing: From Graz come the papers of an earlier victory. In Inner Austria, Ferdinand has seen Protestant schools closed, pastors expelled, town councils altered, and Catholic officeholding rebuilt under the cover of princely right.
situation: The Estates did not vanish. They withheld taxes, petitioned, threatened emigration, and then mostly remained. The lesson carried forward is dangerous because it appears to have worked: prepare carefully, divide provinces, keep within a narrow reading of law, and act once conscience and counsel are aligned.
historian_note: Wilson treats Inner Austria as the formative setting for Ferdinand's legalistic Catholic restoration before the Bohemian crisis.

options.label: Trust the Styrian method: legal commissions, Catholic officeholding, and force when needed.
options.consequence: The archduke's confidence hardens. Restoration can be imagined as obedience to law rather than innovation.

options.label: Use patronage and Catholic appointments, but avoid spectacular expulsions.
options.consequence: Catholic recovery continues more quietly. Zealous advisers ask whether caution has become surrender.

options.label: Seek a new compact with the estates before renewing the commission.
options.consequence: The Estates gain a language of consent. Ferdinand gains fewer enemies and a less certain conscience.

title: Before the Window
briefing: Petitions from Bohemia name Braunau and Klostergrab. Protestant worshippers complain of closed or destroyed churches; royal officials answer that the Letter of Majesty does not protect every disputed site. The matter is carried from local lordship into the language of crown, estate, and privilege.
situation: Ferdinand has been accepted as Bohemian king, and every answer now bears on the future reign. Catholic councillors urge enforcement and the vindication of royal and ecclesiastical rights. Protestant defenders warn that arrests, closures, and royal judges will show that the charter can be reduced by procedure without ever being revoked.
historian_note: Wilson's reading is especially useful here: the Habsburg position was technically legalistic rather than simply lawless, but its political handling was dangerous. That is the central historical tradeoff for this card.

options.label: Confirm the strict legal line and support closures, arrests, and royal judges.
options.consequence: Catholic officials and clergy report that the new king will not retreat from enforcement. Bohemian Protestants carry the orders into their assemblies as evidence that law is being used to narrow the charter by which they still claim obedience.

options.label: Suspend disputed-site enforcement and call for controlled legal clarification.
options.consequence: The petitioners can still tell their assemblies that procedure has force. Catholic allies hear hesitation from a prince whose reputation rests on restoring rights they believe have been usurped.

options.label: Allow Klesl and moderates to seek settlement while reserving royal claims.
options.consequence: Envoys and councillors keep a channel open, and neither side must yet confess defeat. Ferdinand's harder supporters see delay; the more radical Bohemian directors gain time to assemble their own answer.

title: Windows in Prague
briefing: Prague's Protestant estates had spent years treating the Letter of Majesty as a shield for their churches, schools, and political standing. Catholic royal officials narrowed that protection, arrests and closures followed, and a radical group decided to force the crisis into the open.
situation: Royal officials have been thrown from the windows of Prague Castle. The rebels frame the act as defense of estate liberties, religious privilege, and the older royal promises recorded in the Letter of Majesty. Your first response will teach the Empire whether this is a local rebellion, a legal dispute, or the start of a reckoning.
historian_note: The 1609 Letter of Majesty matters here because it turns Bohemian religious claims into a chartered estate-liberty problem: religion, schools, churches, defenders, and recorded royal protection all sit behind the rebels' language of privilege.

options.label: Frame the revolt as a legal breach while reserving chartered Bohemian liberties for review.
options.consequence: The legal line gives cautious estates a reason to stay loyal. Catholic hardliners hear you preserving the very paper they wanted buried.

options.label: Declare the rebels traitors and reject their privilege claims as cover for revolt.
options.consequence: Catholic allies applaud the clarity. Protestant and estate observers hear that a recorded royal promise may not protect them once obedience fails.

options.label: Offer a conference on the Letter of Majesty if the rebels reaffirm Habsburg kingship.
options.consequence: Moderates have a bridge back, but the bridge limits how far victory can later carry Catholic restoration.

title: The Cardinal in the Way
briefing: Reports from Vienna name Cardinal Klesl as the man still pressing for accommodation. His letters and envoys promise obedience if Prague will lay down arms, but the court hears only delay while the directors gather men and money.
situation: Ferdinand's allies demand a clearer hand. Klesl can still speak to moderates, yet every day spent negotiating leaves the revolt in possession of Bohemian offices and presses the Habsburg treasury harder.
historian_note: Backend note: Wilson treats Klesl's removal as a real inflection, but the peace alternative remains inferred and requires later source checking.

options.label: Keep Klesl negotiating and demand that Prague disarm before any further grace.
options.consequence: The court still has a channel to moderate estates, but Catholic advisers complain that time is being granted to men already in arms.

options.label: Remove Klesl from the center of power and prepare a harder answer.
options.consequence: The chancery moves with fewer scruples. The war chest improves, but Prague sees fewer reasons to expect settlement from Vienna.

options.label: Sideline Klesl publicly but use his contacts to keep one door open.
options.consequence: Hardliners hear that Ferdinand is no longer ruled by a cardinal's caution, while Prague receives enough signals to keep bargaining alive.

title: Terms Carried Between Courts
briefing: Klesl's agents keep moving between doubtful nobles, Catholic councillors, and men who still say they fight for privileges rather than against the dynasty.
situation: The offers are narrower than Prague wants and slower than the Catholic party will bear. A settlement may still be written, but only if one side accepts less than it has proclaimed.
historian_note: Backend note: this is a Wilson-inferred alternate branch from Klesl's conciliatory role, not a claim that peace would certainly have followed.

options.label: Accept a narrow settlement if the directors disarm and preserve royal authority.
options.consequence: Moderates gain words they can carry home, but neither the directors nor the Catholic party receive the victory they promised their friends.

options.label: Let the talks fail rather than concede the crown's disputed rights.
options.consequence: The language of negotiation is exhausted. Those who warned that Vienna only meant delay now find easier listeners.

title: The Storm at Vienna
briefing: Thurn has crossed the frontier, and Protestant nobles in Lower Austria press into Ferdinand's presence with demands for security before they will stand obedient.
situation: The palace waits for cavalry that may or may not arrive in time. If Ferdinand yields under pressure, Prague will hear it; if he refuses, Vienna may see how narrow his obedience has become.
historian_note: Backend note: Wilson supports the actual pattern of firmness followed by selective reassurance; broader alternatives are inferred from the pressure field.

options.label: Hold firm until loyal horsemen enter the city.
options.consequence: The petitioners withdraw without a corporate triumph. The danger passes, and their boldest men stand more exposed than before.

options.label: Confirm individual noble privileges in return for homage.
options.consequence: Moderates receive something they can accept without joining Prague. Corporate unity weakens, though the crown admits it must bargain with anxious estates.

options.label: Grant a broader corporate guarantee to quiet Lower Austria.
options.consequence: The immediate danger eases, but Prague learns that armed pressure can draw written security from Ferdinand.

title: The Crown and the Electors
briefing: The Bohemian revolt has survived long enough to become a constitutional challenge. Ferdinand must secure the imperial crown while Prague argues that his Bohemian kingship was conditional, unlawful, or forfeited.
situation: Bohemian estates circulate arguments that you were not freely elected, that your promises were conditional, and that Spanish-Habsburg designs threaten their privileges. Their claims draw strength from an older royal settlement: the Letter of Majesty made religious liberty, schools, churches, and estate defenders part of Bohemia's recorded political order.
historian_note: A 1619 Bohemian estates text frames Ferdinand's problem as legal, confessional, and dynastic, not merely military. The 1609 Letter of Majesty explains why the dispute could be presented as defense of recorded liberties rather than simple disobedience. The likely effects of each response still need direct review in Wilson and Asch.

options.label: Court the electors and make the imperial title the first answer to Prague.
options.consequence: The imperial crown steadies your hand. The estates' charter language still circulates, but you now speak from a higher desk.

options.label: Denounce the estates' reasons as rebellion dressed in charter language.
options.consequence: You refuse to let Prague define the law. Cautious estates hear that old liberties may be judged after obedience, not before it.

options.label: Publish a legal rebuttal and promise a controlled review of Letter-of-Majesty protections.
options.consequence: You answer the estates on their chosen ground. Zealous allies dislike giving rebels the dignity of an argument, and the review may bind your later settlement.

title: Frankfurt's Oath
briefing: Ferdinand has chosen the imperial election as the lever that can turn a dynastic crisis into an imperial-legal crisis. The ceremony gives him authority, but the coronation oath also gives the electors and Estates standards to invoke against him.
situation: Frankfurt gives you ceremony, regalia, electors, ambassadors, acclamation, and oath. The same pamphlet that reports the coronation also carries the noise of Bohemian and Austrian crisis: armed pressure, failed Protestant-Catholic agreement, and demands that privileges be secured. The crown can answer Prague, but it can also give Prague and every elector an oath to measure you by.
historian_note: The English news pamphlet is useful because it places the coronation beside active crisis reporting and describes the public machinery of legitimacy: elector and ambassador roles, Golden Bull offices, regalia, acclamation, and oaths. It proves contemporary framing and ceremony, not the deeper causal weight of the coronation; that still needs direct comparison with modern scholarship.

options.label: Use Frankfurt as proof that Prague now defies the lawful emperor.
options.consequence: The crown raises your voice above the Bohemian estates. It also makes every coercive move sound like an imperial precedent, not merely a dynastic quarrel.

options.label: Publish the coronation as a promise of law, consultation, and protected privilege.
options.consequence: Moderate estates gain language for loyalty without surrendering every fear. Catholic allies hear the new emperor tying his own hands before the fight is won.

options.label: Keep the imperial ceremony separate from Bohemia and avoid turning the revolt into an imperial test case.
options.consequence: You reduce the sense that the new crown is aimed straight at Prague. You also leave your opponents more room to argue that the Bohemian dispute stands on its own law.

title: The Bavarian Bargain
briefing: The imperial title has not produced an army. Bohemia, Transylvania, and Frederick's supporters create an immediate force problem, and Maximilian of Bavaria is the Catholic prince most able to solve it quickly.
situation: You need an army before Bohemia's revolt hardens into a new order. Maximilian of Bavaria and the Catholic League can provide force, but the Munich Treaty terms would give Bavaria a hand in command, compensation, and any later settlement.
historian_note: Valeš's legal-history article reads the 1619 Munich Treaty as an emergency bargain: Maximilian receives direction of Catholic defense preparations, Ferdinand accepts compensation obligations, and Article II restricts separate negotiation, peace, or truces with Protestants without Bavarian knowledge and cooperation. The treaty text itself is still an acquisition target, while Ferdinand's 1619 election capitulation adds the constitutional pressure that war, burdens, alliances, and legitimacy must still look lawful.

options.label: Accept Maximilian's Munich terms for League command and compensation.
options.consequence: Bavarian columns give your cause teeth. Maximilian now has a claim on command, compensation, and any peace table.

options.label: Seek broader elector and Catholic-estate subscription first.
options.consequence: Dependence is spread more widely and looks more constitutional, but Maximilian's army is slower to move and ready money remains scarce.

options.label: Refuse separate-peace limits and build an imperial force.
options.consequence: You preserve more imperial freedom, but the Bohemian and Transylvanian emergencies do not wait for a cleaner army.

memory_variants.briefing: Munich's hand is already strengthened. Since the court treated Catholic association as the necessary answer to Protestant coordination, Maximilian and the League now appear less as petitioners than as the instrument already chosen for rescue.
memory_variants.situation: Bohemia, Transylvania, and Frederick's supporters still create an immediate force problem. The price is sharper: Bavarian command, compensation, and a voice in settlement now follow from an earlier policy as well as from present necessity.

memory_variants.briefing: Because the leagues were tolerated as emergency instruments under imperial law, Munich can offer aid in the same guarded language. Maximilian and the Catholic League promise rescue while professing obedience to the public peace.
memory_variants.situation: The offer is useful because it looks lawful; it is dangerous because the army that saves Bohemia will also carry claims for command, compensation, and consultation.

memory_variants.briefing: The earlier condemnation of the leagues now returns as difficulty. Maximilian can still help, but the court must explain why Catholic armed association is unlawful in principle and indispensable in practice.
memory_variants.situation: Bohemia requires force before ordinary imperial levies can answer. Accepting Bavarian aid under these conditions risks making necessity stronger than the very law invoked against faction.

title: Saxony and the Union
briefing: Ferdinand cannot afford to let the Bohemian conflict become a unified Protestant cause. Saxony's elector dislikes Calvinist radicalism and values imperial order, but he also needs visible protection for Lutheran rights.
situation: John George of Saxony is Lutheran, but he fears disorder and values imperial legality. He may help isolate Frederick if you make this a question of law rather than a Catholic crusade.
historian_note: Saxony is modeled as a legalist Protestant power, not as a simple confessional enemy. The election capitulation gives Ferdinand a direct vocabulary for reassurance: religious peace, Landfrieden, estate rights, and due process.

options.label: Promise Saxony that the religious peace and estate rights will be respected.
options.consequence: Saxon cooperation becomes easier. Catholic hardliners mutter that the emperor bargains with heresy.

options.label: Pressure Saxony to prove loyalty before debating legal assurances.
options.consequence: You assert imperial command, but Saxony hears obedience being placed before the law you swore to uphold.

options.label: Let Bavaria and Catholic allies carry the matter; Saxony can follow or stand aside.
options.consequence: Catholic unity is cleaner. Protestant reassurance is not, and the electoral-constitutional language that could isolate Frederick goes unused.

title: The Road to Prague
briefing: The allied armies have forced the revolt backward, but the commanders disagree over the next stroke. Bucquoy looks toward Moravia; Tilly and Maximilian press the road to Prague.
situation: Winter approaches. A direct march may make the Bohemian crown fall in one blow, or leave the army before a hard city in bad season.
historian_note: Backend note: Wilson supports the actual direct march and political collapse; alternate campaign outcomes remain inferred.

options.label: Follow Tilly and Maximilian toward Prague.
options.consequence: The army moves where court and crown can be broken together. Success will make the field battle a political judgment.

options.label: Follow Bucquoy's slower Moravian approach.
options.consequence: The campaign promises firmer ground and fewer winter hazards, but Prague is given more time to gather courage, coin, and allies.

options.label: Pause for winter and consolidate allied positions.
options.consequence: The army is spared a hazardous finish, but victory loses its terror and the confederates keep a court around Frederick.

title: After White Mountain
briefing: Bavarian and imperial force has broken the rebel army outside Prague. Frederick has fled, but the victory now has to be translated into law, punishment, property, and obedience.
situation: The rebel army has been broken outside Prague. Victory is real, but its meaning is undecided. Punishment, mercy, confiscation, and restoration all point toward different futures.
historian_note: The card does not assume victory automatically produces stability. It asks what kind of victory Ferdinand makes.

options.label: Name leading rebels for exemplary punishment while preserving pardon for lesser estates.
options.consequence: Habsburg command tightens. The lesson travels farther than Prague.

options.label: Punish leaders but preserve enough law to separate rebels from estates.
options.consequence: Your settlement is severe but legible. It leaves less fuel for moderates to panic.

options.label: Offer broad amnesty to estates that swear renewed obedience.
options.consequence: Fear recedes, but Catholic allies see a chance for restoration slipping away.

title: The Blood Court
briefing: The Prague court has named traitors and delivered death sentences. Petitions and advisers reach Ferdinand before the warrants leave Vienna.
situation: The revolt may be taught by spectacle, or punished by property, exile, and oath. The square in Prague waits for the form of obedience the emperor will command.
historian_note: Backend note: Wilson explicitly calls the executions unnecessary and a mistake, making this a high-confidence alternate branch.

options.label: Sign the exemplary death warrants.
options.consequence: The punishment is made visible before Prague. Fear enters the settlement, and exile memory hardens around the scaffold.

options.label: Commute most sentences and reserve death for the most prominent cases.
options.consequence: The court still marks treason, but Prague sees that obedience need not end on the scaffold for every condemned man.

options.label: Use humiliation, exile, and confiscation instead of executions.
options.consequence: Lives are spared while names and lands are struck. Hardliners call it weakness, but fewer households receive martyrs.

title: Lands for Loyalty
briefing: The crown has defeated the revolt, but it still owes soldiers, allies, and loyal nobles. Rebel property offers money and reward, while every confiscation teaches the defeated what Habsburg victory means.
situation: Confiscated rebel property can pay debts, reward loyalists, and remake Bohemia's ruling class. It can also convince every estate that defeat means social death.
historian_note: Confiscation is modeled as fiscal policy, social transformation, and a fear signal at once.

options.label: Use large confiscations to reward loyal Catholics and fund the settlement.
options.consequence: Money and loyalty flow through confiscated land. So does terror of imperial victory.

options.label: Confiscate selectively and keep a public legal record of each case.
options.consequence: The settlement pays less quickly, but it looks less like appetite wearing a crown.

options.label: Commute many confiscations to fines and renewed oaths.
options.consequence: You collect less and transform less, but you leave more people with something to lose by rebelling again.

title: The Spanish Road
briefing: The Palatine question pulls the war toward the Rhine, where Spanish Habsburg interests and the Dutch war matter. Ferdinand's family can help, but their help makes the imperial crisis look European.
situation: Spanish Habsburg interests align with yours against Frederick, but their Rhine concerns are tied to the Dutch war. Help from Madrid can make the Palatinate a European hinge.
historian_note: The card abstracts Spanish Habsburg strategic interest without pretending the Empire and Spain had identical goals. Ferdinand's capitulation makes foreign alliances and foreign troops a constitutional sensitivity, not merely a diplomatic preference.

options.label: Coordinate closely with Spain in the Palatinate and along the Rhine.
options.consequence: Dynastic power gathers. So do the anxieties of every power watching the Rhine.

options.label: Accept Spanish help quietly but keep imperial policy visibly separate.
options.consequence: You gain some help without making the Empire look like Madrid's instrument.

options.label: Keep Spain at arm's length and frame the matter as purely imperial.
options.consequence: The legal story is cleaner. The practical resources are thinner.

title: Who Pays the League?
briefing: Victory has not ended the bills. The League, imperial officers, creditors, and occupied territories all press on the same fragile fiscal system.
situation: Armies do not live on legitimacy. The Catholic League expects support, officers expect pay, and territories under contribution feel the war in barns and town halls.
historian_note: This card makes finance a central political constraint rather than a background number.

options.label: Authorize heavier contributions from occupied and loyal territories alike.
options.consequence: The army stays fed. The countryside learns that loyalty is not immunity.

options.label: Borrow against future confiscations and dynastic credit.
options.consequence: You spare some immediate suffering, but the court's future narrows around debt.

options.label: Limit campaign aims until finance catches up with ambition.
options.consequence: The war breathes. Your allies ask why they fought to stop short.

title: The Ban of Frederick
briefing: White Mountain has made Frederick vulnerable, but legal punishment of an elector is not ordinary discipline. Ferdinand must make the ban look like lawful imperial defense rather than raw Habsburg revenge.
situation: Frederick has fled, but not vanished. His claim still gathers money, men, and sympathy. Your chancery can name him an outlaw of the Empire and command every subject, estate, officer, and vassal to deny him aid.
historian_note: This card is grounded in Ferdinand's 22 January 1621 imperial-ban declaration, read against the 1619 capitulation's due-process promise. The decree says Frederick had incurred the Landfrieden penalties ipso facto, yet Ferdinand still issues a confirming declaration; that is exactly where legal force and process anxiety meet. The documents prove Ferdinand's legal framing and constitutional constraint, not by themselves how every estate interpreted the ban.

options.label: Declare Frederick under the imperial and upper ban.
options.consequence: Your victory gains legal teeth. But every estate now studies whether cause, hearing, and process can bend under pressure.

options.label: Offer pardon if Frederick renounces Bohemia and disarms.
options.consequence: Moderates see an exit from the crisis. Catholic allies see a rebel king being given one more door.

options.label: Outlaw Frederick, but publicly reassure neutral princes and Palatine subjects.
options.consequence: The decree isolates one man instead of threatening every estate. This restraint will need allies willing to obey the legal boundary.

title: The Paladins Remain in the Field
briefing: Heidelberg and Mannheim have fallen, yet the Palatine cause has not laid down its arms. Mansfeld and Christian of Brunswick still carry war through the Empire, while English and Spanish envoys look for terms they can call peace.
situation: Ferdinand may punish Frederick, bargain over restoration, or separate lesser supporters from the elector's ruin. Every course touches Maximilian's expected reward.
historian_note: Backend note: replaces the duplicate 1622 Frederick-ban card with Wilson's Regensburg and Palatine settlement problem.

options.label: Offer conditional restoration if Frederick renounces Bohemia and his commanders disband.
options.consequence: The Palatine grievance is given a road back into law, but Maximilian hears that victory may not bring the full price promised at Munich.

options.label: Keep the ban in force and pursue military settlement.
options.consequence: No prince mistakes Ferdinand's victory for weakness, but the Palatine name remains useful to every foreign patron seeking an imperial grievance.

options.label: Separate Frederick's punishment from amnesty for lesser Palatine supporters.
options.consequence: The elector remains marked, but lesser men are offered a way home. The exile network loses some breadth without satisfying Frederick's closest allies.

options.label: Use Spanish and Bavarian pressure to force a settlement favorable to the Habsburgs.
options.consequence: Allied force drives the settlement forward, but the Empire sees that Palatine law now moves in the shadow of Madrid and Munich.

title: Maximilian's Price
briefing: Bavaria helped save Ferdinand when his own resources were thin. The earlier bargain now comes due in the Palatinate, where rewarding Maximilian means altering the electoral balance of the Empire.
situation: Maximilian did not save your cause as an act of poetry. The secret promise behind the Bavarian bargain now presses forward: Palatine lands and Frederick's electoral dignity can reward Bavaria, punish rebellion, and remake the balance among electors.
historian_note: Valeš connects the 1623 settlement to an earlier secret oral promise attached to the 1619 Munich Treaty: Ferdinand offered Maximilian the Palatine electoral dignity and conquered Palatine territories, while knowing the promise exceeded his legal competence and would alarm German princes. The transfer option follows the historical direction; alternatives are plausible game abstractions, not asserted certainties.

options.label: Fulfill the promise and transfer the electoral dignity to Maximilian.
options.consequence: Bavaria is rewarded and Catholic victory is crowned. The electors see that an emergency bargain can become a new constitutional fact.

options.label: Delay the dignity while granting Bavaria security and revenues.
options.consequence: The constitutional shock is softened, but Maximilian's patience becomes another debt with interest.

options.label: Punish Frederick but preserve the electoral balance for now.
options.consequence: Electors are reassured by restraint, and Bavaria is not. A disappointed ally is still an armed ally.
options.unavailable_text: Bavarian claims now bind the settlement too tightly for a balance policy to be credible.

memory_variants.title: Maximilian's Claim
memory_variants.briefing: Regensburg has not ended Bavaria's claim. Maximilian's soldiers and credit helped recover the emperor's position, and Munich's promise still stands over every Palatine compromise.
memory_variants.situation: A softer Palatine settlement leaves Ferdinand with a different danger: if Frederick is not utterly stripped, Bavaria must still be satisfied without making the electoral college look disposable.

pressure_variants.briefing: The memorials from Munich no longer read as requests. They read as accounts due. Maximilian's service in Bohemia, the League's expense, and the unsettled Palatine title are now presented together.
pressure_variants.situation: The electors hear that the emperor must reward useful loyalty, but several courts warn that an electoral title cannot be moved without wounding the balance of the Empire.

title: A Victory That Will Not End
briefing: By 1623, Ferdinand has survived the opening crisis and punished the Bohemian-Palatine challenge. Yet the settlement leaves debts, displaced elites, anxious princes, and allies who expect rewards.
situation: Bohemia is subdued and Frederick is broken, yet the Empire is not calm. Every settlement creates a constituency: rewarded allies, frightened estates, ruined towns, unpaid soldiers, and watching foreign powers.
historian_note: This closing MVP card asks whether the player has made consolidation or escalation more likely.

options.label: Call for a formal imperial settlement to lock in obedience and reassure moderates.
options.consequence: You try to turn victory back into law. It is slower than command but less combustible.

options.label: Keep pressure on remaining opposition until no prince doubts imperial reach.
options.consequence: Authority looks grand from Vienna. From Protestant courts, it looks like a forecast.

options.label: Demobilize what you can and spend political capital on fiscal repair.
options.consequence: The war machine cools, but allies and officers who profited from motion resist stillness.

title: Lower Saxony Will Not Stay Quiet
briefing: Letters from the north report assemblies claiming neutrality while Danish agents speak of protection, bishoprics, and the defence of endangered estates.
situation: If neutrality is accepted without condition, an imperial circle may decide when imperial law binds it. If it is refused, Denmark may enter not as a distant king but as armed guardian of a threatened frontier.
historian_note: Wilson frames the Danish-Lower Saxon phase around neutrality, bishoprics, circle politics, and imperial authority.

options.label: Refuse a neutrality that shelters Denmark's cause.
options.consequence: Imperial orders speak of common liberty and obedience. Northern estates hear command; Denmark hears invitation.

options.label: Recognize a temporary Kreis neutrality under imperial review.
options.consequence: The north breathes for a season, but Catholic petitioners ask whether imperial law now waits upon every circle's convenience.

options.label: Let League pressure compel the wavering estates.
options.consequence: The language of law arrives with soldiers behind it. The warning is clear, and so is the danger.

title: A Field Army of Ferdinand's Own
briefing: A proposal reaches court promising men faster than the treasury can pay them. Credit, commissions, contributions, and the commander's name will do what ordinary revenue cannot.
situation: The emperor can remain dependent on Bavaria and the League, or he can accept an army whose purse lies in the lands it occupies and whose officers look upward through Wallenstein.
historian_note: Wilson treats Wallenstein's system as both capacity solution and autonomous military-fiscal network.

pressure_variants.briefing: The treasury figures arrive in a poor hand and worse news. Arrears, pledges, and ally claims leave little room for an ordinary imperial army.

options.label: Accept Wallenstein's contribution army.
options.consequence: Recruiting begins with astonishing speed. So do complaints from the lands asked to feed it.

options.label: Authorize a smaller army under tighter warrants.
options.consequence: The court keeps the commander on a shorter leash, and receives a smaller instrument in return.

options.label: Remain with League and Spanish support rather than build a new system.
options.consequence: Maximilian's value rises again. The emperor avoids one dangerous servant by leaning harder on another ally.

title: Frederick Nearly Bends
briefing: After Danish reverses, word arrives that Frederick will yield more than before: Bohemia renounced, Maximilian accepted for life, submission offered by proxy.
situation: The remaining question is not whether Frederick loses face, but how much face the emperor requires him to lose in public before peace can be made.
historian_note: Wilson notes that agreement was close, but Ferdinand's demand for personal submission helped close the opening.

options.label: Require Frederick's personal submission to imperial authority.
options.consequence: The dignity of punishment is preserved. The settlement slips away on the form of obedience.

options.label: Accept proxy submission and secure the renunciations.
options.consequence: A humiliating journey is spared. Bavaria asks what certainty remains when rebellion can be softened by parchment.

options.label: Trade limited restoration for security and reparations.
options.consequence: The Palatine cause is divided from the mercenary war, but every clause must pass through Bavarian suspicion.

title: Mandates in the Hereditary Lands
briefing: Reports from Bohemia, Moravia, and Austria list pastors removed, churches inspected, offices watched, and noble houses pressed toward conformity.
situation: Catholic loyalists ask that victory now be made visible in worship, schooling, marriage, office, and landholding. Other advisers warn that sudden uniformity will send property, labor, and hatred abroad with the exiles.
historian_note: This card previews later overreach dynamics without jumping ahead to the Edict of Restitution.

options.label: Encourage visible Catholic restoration in recovered lands.
options.consequence: Catholic confidence surges. Protestant alarm learns to organize itself.

options.label: Sequence restoration slowly, after oaths and fiscal order.
options.consequence: The settlement advances, but not fast enough for the most zealous allies.

options.label: Suspend major restoration measures to calm Lutheran and city opinion.
options.consequence: Moderates breathe easier. Catholic allies wonder what victory was for.

title: Mecklenburg as Payment
briefing: The commander who raised the army now seeks a reward large enough to satisfy credit, honor, and arrears. Mecklenburg lies under imperial displeasure.
situation: To pay with land is easier than paying with money. It also tells every prince that victory may move old houses out and new servants in.
historian_note: Wilson presents Wallenstein's elevation in Mecklenburg as a key overreach signal.

options.label: Grant Mecklenburg to Wallenstein.
options.consequence: The army's maker is paid in princely coin. The Empire studies the precedent with fear.

options.label: Grant administration without hereditary title.
options.consequence: Wallenstein receives substance without the full shock of a ducal transfer. The distinction satisfies few, but alarms fewer.

options.label: Seek cash and movable confiscations instead.
options.consequence: The old dynastic order is spared a warning, but the treasury groans and the army waits.
options.unavailable_text: The treasury cannot credibly satisfy Wallenstein's arrears without using land, offices, or future contributions.

title: Peace at Lubeck
briefing: Christian of Denmark has lost the mainland war but not his kingdom. Negotiators ask whether the emperor wants vengeance, compensation, or one enemy removed before Sweden moves.
situation: A generous peace can look like weakness to friends expecting spoils. A punitive peace can keep Denmark in the field when the north is already too open.
historian_note: Wilson emphasizes the generosity and strategic logic of Lubeck, especially the wish to remove Denmark.

options.label: Return Danish provinces if Christian abandons the Lower Saxons.
options.consequence: Denmark leaves the war. The abandoned estates learn what imperial peace costs them.

options.label: Demand compensation and sharper guarantees.
options.consequence: Friends applaud a harder peace. Denmark hesitates, and Swedish calculations improve.

options.label: Use Lubeck to open a general imperial settlement.
options.consequence: The war party complains that victory is being spent too cheaply; moderates see the first real door in years.
options.unavailable_text: Too much alarm has gathered for a general settlement to be credible without first quieting Protestant security fears.

title: The Edict of Restitution
briefing: Imperial victories over Bohemia, the Palatinate, and Denmark make a definitive religious settlement look possible. The danger is that a legal triumph may frighten the very Lutheran princes needed for peace.
situation: Victory has made the old religious settlement look enforceable again. Your jurists say the Peace of Augsburg, the imperial records, and your election oath give you enough ground to restore ecclesiastical goods through commissioners.
historian_note: This card is grounded in Ferdinand's Edict of Restitution. The source gives the official legal-confessional case; the wider causal consequences still need direct review in modern scholarship.

options.label: Issue the edict and send commissioners to enforce restitution.
options.consequence: Catholic restoration gains the force of imperial office. Protestant estates hear the settlement being rewritten from Vienna.

options.label: Seek elector or Diet-backed interpretation before execution.
options.consequence: The law remains more shared, but restoration slows and Catholic allies see victory losing its nerve.

options.label: Enforce only the clearest restitution cases for now.
options.consequence: The edict has teeth, but not yet jaws. Everyone presses you to define what comes next.

options.label: Use restitution claims as bargaining material for a wider peace.
options.consequence: The Empire may breathe. The most committed Catholic restorers will remember what you left on the table.
options.unavailable_text: Trust has fallen too low, or foreign danger has risen too far, for restitution to buy peace by bargain alone.

memory_variants.briefing: The generous peace at Lubeck has removed Denmark without opening a general settlement. Catholic petitioners now press that victory and peace together should permit the old church claims to be made good.
memory_variants.situation: A decree can satisfy those claims, but the same paper may tell Lutheran princes that moderation toward Denmark was only preparation for enforcement inside the Empire.

memory_variants.briefing: Mandates in the hereditary lands have already made Catholic restoration visible in churches, schools, offices, and noble houses. The question now arrives in imperial form.
memory_variants.situation: To issue an Edict is to carry the hereditary method into the wider Empire; to delay is to disappoint those who believed victory had proved the method lawful.

memory_variants.briefing: The earlier willingness to accept proxy submission in the Palatine matter has preserved a language of settlement. The restitution petitions now test whether that restraint can survive Catholic victory.
memory_variants.situation: A broad Edict would reverse the tone of compromise. A narrower interpretation may keep wavering Lutheran estates from treating every imperial paper as threat.

title: Regensburg: The Price of Consent
briefing: Electoral complaints arrive in a single chorus: contributions, Mecklenburg, the army, the Edict, and Wallenstein's shadow over imperial liberties.
situation: Ferdinand seeks consent and dynastic advantage. The electors answer that consent begins with the dismissal of the man who made imperial victory so frightening.
historian_note: Wilson treats Regensburg as collective imperial politics checking Ferdinand's overreach.

options.label: Dismiss Wallenstein to recover electoral consent.
options.consequence: The electors receive the sacrifice. Sweden receives a less ready enemy.

options.label: Keep Wallenstein with reduced powers.
options.consequence: The army remains; consent thins. The congress begins to look less like settlement than warning.

options.label: Offer army reform in exchange for succession support.
options.consequence: The bargain protects the dynasty more than the field army. It buys time, not peace.

title: The Door Stands Open
briefing: Reports from Saxony and the Protestant estates no longer ask only for delay. They speak of armed security, lawful defence, and the Swedish king already on imperial soil.
situation: If Ferdinand offers no public settlement, the middle party may cease to be middle. If he yields too much, Catholic allies ask what victory and law were for.
historian_note: Wilson says Ferdinand's refusal of the Leipzig off-ramp compounded the Edict error and helped drive Saxony toward Sweden.

options.label: Reject Leipzig and command disarmament.
options.consequence: Saxon neutrality breaks under the weight of command. Sweden gains the ally it needed.

options.label: Suspend the Edict and accept Saxon mediation.
options.consequence: The Catholic party murmurs, but the Lutheran elector remains reachable.

options.label: Offer private concessions while refusing a public bloc.
options.consequence: The court tries to buy trust without admitting necessity. The answer depends on how much trust remains.

memory_variants.briefing: The Edict now travels ahead of every imperial envoy. Reports from Saxony and the Protestant estates no longer ask only for delay; they ask whether obedience can coexist with armed security.
memory_variants.situation: The Swedish king is already on imperial soil. If Ferdinand offers no public settlement, the middle party may cease to be middle; if he yields too much, Catholic allies ask what victory and law were for.

memory_variants.briefing: Because restitution was treated as peace business rather than command alone, Saxon envoys still have language enough to ask for public terms before they choose arms.
memory_variants.situation: The Swedish king is already on imperial soil, but the Lutheran middle has not yet lost every reason to bargain with the emperor.

title: Saxony Crosses the Line
briefing: New dispatches report that Saxon counsel no longer trusts suspension by private word. The Edict remains public, Leipzig has been refused, and Swedish arms now offer the security that imperial law no longer seems to provide.
situation: John George's step does not make Saxony a natural rebel. It shows that a loyal Lutheran elector can be driven from guarded obedience into armed partnership when the terms of obedience look unsafe.
historian_note: Wilson links Ferdinand's refusal of the Leipzig off-ramp to Saxony's movement toward Sweden after the Edict of Restitution had already frightened Lutheran moderates.

options.label: Treat the Saxon alignment as rebellion and prepare for a wider imperial war.
options.consequence: The court preserves the language of command. The price is that one more elector's obedience must now be recovered by arms.

options.label: Send public suspension terms to separate Saxony from Sweden.
options.consequence: Envoys carry a late offer that may loosen Saxon commitment but cannot erase the proof that armed pressure forced the paper.

title: Gollersdorf
briefing: After Swedish victories, the dismissed general receives visitors again. He will not return as a mere servant who can be corrected by every ally's complaint.
situation: The army can be restored quickly only by granting powers that make the court uneasy. Without him, Bavaria and scattered commands must carry the war.
historian_note: Wilson presents Wallenstein's recall as necessity joined to broad delegation.

options.label: Recall Wallenstein with broad Gollersdorf powers.
options.consequence: The imperial army gathers around its old magnet. So do old fears.

options.label: Recall him under written limits.
options.consequence: The court asks for a safer miracle. Wallenstein weighs whether such a command is worth taking.

options.label: Build a coalition command without him.
options.consequence: The old dependency returns under worse circumstances. Maximilian is necessary again.

title: The General Makes His Own Peace
briefing: Wallenstein's letters and silences grow harder to read. Some reports say he seeks settlement; others say he seeks command of the settlement itself.
situation: To tolerate his diplomacy may split the enemy. To supervise it may provoke him. To prepare alternatives may turn suspicion into rupture.
historian_note: Wilson treats Wallenstein's opaque diplomacy as a real source of mistrust even if outright treason remains difficult to prove cleanly.

options.label: Build Spanish and Bavarian alternatives to Wallenstein.
options.consequence: Trust becomes a military plan. The general reads the plan as accusation.

options.label: Authorize his peace soundings under explicit warrant.
options.consequence: The court turns danger into instrument, but every ally fears what the instrument may sign.

options.label: Confront and renegotiate his powers.
options.consequence: The wound is opened before the army chooses sides.

title: Dead or Alive
briefing: Patents are drafted releasing officers from obedience. The matter can be made legal in form only if the army first ceases to be his.
situation: An arrest risks delay, trial, and exposure. A removal by force recovers command swiftly, but the chancery will inherit the stain.
historian_note: Wilson describes Ferdinand's patents and the political burial after Eger.

options.label: Release the officers and authorize dead-or-alive removal.
options.consequence: Wallenstein falls at Eger. The army returns to obedience; the papers do not return to innocence.

options.label: Arrest him for trial before imperial authority.
options.consequence: The legal road is cleaner and slower. Every day gives the army time to ask whom it serves.

options.label: Reconcile and narrow his command.
options.consequence: The crisis is postponed inside a smaller circle. Bavaria and Spain do not mistake postponement for safety.

title: The Peace of Prague
briefing: After Nordlingen, Saxon articles come within reach. The Edict can be quieted, armies joined under emperor and Empire, and many Lutheran estates brought home.
situation: The danger lies in the names left outside the pardon. Every excluded prince, exile, and army becomes useful to France or Sweden.
historian_note: Wilson calls Prague a broad settlement undermined by exclusions.

options.label: Make the elector peace and exclude the hard cases.
options.consequence: Saxony returns. The excluded learn that foreign protection is now their last court of appeal.

options.label: Broaden the amnesty while protecting core loyalist rewards.
options.consequence: The settlement cuts deeper into the enemy's German support, but loyal beneficiaries ask which promises still hold.
options.unavailable_text: Too much trust has been spent for a broad amnesty to command belief.

options.label: Use Nordlingen to demand a harder Catholic settlement.
options.consequence: Victory is spent like a confession of strength. The peace party thins; foreign patrons gain clients.

memory_variants.briefing: After Wallenstein's violent removal and Nordlingen's victory, Saxon articles come within reach. The court can speak again of imperial order, but officers and princes remember how command was recovered.
memory_variants.situation: The Edict can be quieted, armies joined under emperor and Empire, and many Lutheran estates brought home. The danger lies in the names left outside the pardon.

memory_variants.briefing: Because restitution was already treated as negotiable peace business, the Saxon articles now arrive less as surrender than as a form the court has made possible.
memory_variants.situation: The settlement can restore obedience widely, but every excluded prince, exile, and army remains useful to France or Sweden.

title: The Amnesty Question
briefing: Hessen-Kassel still has soldiers, claims, and foreign suitors. Provisional acceptance of Prague will not become obedience unless terms are made real.
situation: To press Westphalian bishoprics may satisfy friends and reopen war. To concede enough may remove an armed enemy while teaching every holdout to bargain.
historian_note: Wilson treats Hessen-Kassel as a missed chance after Prague.

options.label: Hold the line and let the deal fail if Wilhelm will not yield enough.
options.consequence: The ban follows. Hessen returns to the anti-imperial war with a sharper grievance.

options.label: Offer security concessions to close the Hessen deal.
options.consequence: One dangerous army may be removed from the enemy list. Friends with claims in the region count the cost.

options.label: Use military pressure to compel obedience.
options.consequence: The settlement speaks with cannon behind it. The war in the west hardens.

title: Regensburg Again
briefing: The emperor's health is no longer a private matter. The electors can secure Ferdinand's son, but they can also write new restraints into the price of continuity.
situation: To delay is to gamble with succession. To press forward is to accept that the next emperor will inherit both the crown and the conditions attached to it.
historian_note: Wilson treats Ferdinand III's election as dynastic success bound by consultation limits and unresolved war.

options.label: Secure Ferdinand III's election as king of the Romans.
options.consequence: The dynasty survives the emperor's body. The war survives the dynasty's success.

options.label: Buy warmer consent with broader procedural guarantees.
options.consequence: The election becomes less brittle and the crown less free.

options.label: Delay the election until military fortunes improve.
options.consequence: The chancery gains negotiating room and loses sleep. Every fever now has constitutional meaning.

title: Credit Still Offered by the Estates
briefing: Several moderate estates answer that imperial terms can still be carried into their diets, provided old liberties are named rather than swallowed in silence.
situation: This credit is not affection. It is a usable belief that obedience may still preserve privilege, confession, and local jurisdiction better than armed refusal.
historian_note: Wilson repeatedly emphasizes that imperial government depended on cooperation by estates and princes, not command alone.

options.label: Use the opening to put disputed claims before a controlled diet.
options.consequence: The court spends trust on procedure. More estates remain reachable, though zealous councillors complain that law is being made slow just when victory should speak clearly.

options.label: Preserve the opening for a later settlement rather than spend it at once.
options.consequence: The court avoids a quarrel today. The estates' confidence remains useful, but petitioners who expected action begin counting delay as policy.

title: Guarantees Before Obedience
briefing: Petitions arrive asking not for favor but for written security. Estates that once disputed policy now ask what prevents any privilege from being narrowed after submission.
situation: Every concession now looks like admission of weakness, and every refusal strengthens the argument that only armed guarantees can preserve liberties.
historian_note: The game abstracts Wilson's wider constitutional point: fear of overreach made settlement harder even after imperial victories.

options.label: Offer written guarantees while preserving obedience in form.
options.consequence: Some moderates receive language they can carry home. Catholic hardliners and victorious officers hear that rebellion has taught the court to bargain.

options.label: Refuse guarantees and insist that obedience precede every privilege.
options.consequence: The court keeps the order of authority intact. The petitions leave unanswered, and foreign patrons gain another file of grievances.

title: Arrears on Every Table
briefing: Paymasters, colonels, creditors, and allied agents arrive with the same account in different hands. Soldiers can be promised discipline, but not fed by paper.
situation: The question before council is no longer how to finance policy. It is which policy survives the arrears.
historian_note: Wilson treats war finance and contribution systems as central to the war's political escalation.

options.label: Authorize heavier contributions until pay can be restored.
options.consequence: The army stays in being by pressing the lands harder. Every requisition makes the emperor's war visible in barns, cellars, and town accounts.

options.label: Disband unreliable companies and save credit for the core army.
options.consequence: The treasury breathes a little. Commanders protest, allies doubt the army's reach, and the crown accepts a smaller instrument.

title: Ready Money, Rare Freedom
briefing: The treasury is not rich, but it can still answer a demand without granting land, title, or command in place of coin.
situation: Money gives the court a kind of liberty that victory alone does not: the ability to refuse some dangerous bargains.
historian_note: This is a game abstraction from Wilson's emphasis on the political power created by fiscal scarcity.

options.label: Use ready credit to keep military rewards within ordinary grants.
options.consequence: Officers grumble less when paid, and fewer servants need to be made princes. The treasury buys constitutional quiet at real cost.

options.label: Reserve credit for succession and diplomacy.
options.consequence: The court keeps money for the next bargain. Commanders notice that their accounts remain second to dynastic business.

title: The Price of Armed Servants
briefing: The men who keep armies in the field now send counsel as well as accounts. They ask whether policy will follow the soldiers who make policy possible.
situation: To refuse them risks the instrument of survival. To satisfy them teaches every prince that imperial necessity can be made to pay.
historian_note: This abstracts the recurring Bavarian and Wallenstein problem: military capacity could become leverage over imperial policy.

options.label: Satisfy the armed creditors before they become rivals.
options.consequence: The army remains usable, but obedience is purchased in public view. The price of survival becomes a precedent.

options.label: Reassert command and risk a break with military creditors.
options.consequence: The court reminds servants that credit is not sovereignty. The reminder is lawful, dangerous, and expensive if the army hesitates.

date_label: When foreign intervention risk is extreme
title: Foreign Courts Find Their Cause
briefing: Envoys report that imperial quarrels are being translated abroad into the language of balance, protection, recovery, and religion.
situation: The court may still claim domestic law. Other crowns now answer that domestic law has become a European danger.
historian_note: Wilson frames the widening war as a fusion of imperial settlement, dynastic security, and foreign-policy calculation.

options.label: Send public reassurances to deny foreign courts their pretext.
options.consequence: The papers make intervention harder to justify, but they also bind the emperor to words that allies and estates will quote back at him.

options.label: Answer foreign pressure by seeking a decisive military demonstration.
options.consequence: Victory might silence patrons and clients together. Failure would prove that the Empire has become Europe's battlefield.

title: A Crown Not Yet in Panic
briefing: Councillors note that succession no longer has to be bought in the same breath as every military demand. The dynasty has room to choose its concessions.
situation: Security can make moderation easier, but it can also tempt the court to spend less on settlement because the house itself is safe.
historian_note: This is the reward side of Ferdinand's dynastic problem: security changes what concessions are politically bearable.

options.label: Use dynastic security to offer wider settlement terms.
options.consequence: The court can concede without sounding desperate. Catholic allies complain, but some estates hear strength rather than retreat.

options.label: Guard dynastic security and make fewer settlement promises.
options.consequence: The house remains safer, but the Empire hears less of reconciliation and more of continuity.

title: The Lands Petition Against Ruin
briefing: Town councils, territorial officers, and ecclesiastical administrators send reports that no longer separate war policy from hunger, flight, billeting, and unpaid contribution.
situation: Devastation has become an argument in council. Even loyal men ask what obedience can mean if the lands that obey are consumed.
historian_note: Wilson treats wartime devastation and material exhaustion as political facts, not merely background suffering.

options.label: Order relief and contribution limits in the worst-hit lands.
options.consequence: The order gives loyal estates words to defend obedience. Commanders answer that armies cannot march on mercy alone.

options.label: Keep contributions flowing until peace is closer.
options.consequence: The army remains supplied, and the petitions grow darker. Peace itself begins to look like the only relief still credible.

title: The Emperor Dies
briefing: Ferdinand dies with Bohemia held, the dynasty continued, and Catholic restoration rooted deeply in the hereditary lands.
situation: The Empire is not at peace. Every unresolved file passes to Ferdinand III: amnesty, armies, foreign crowns, devastated lands, and the question of how much imperial authority can bear before it breaks cooperation.
historian_note: Wilson marks Ferdinand II's death as dynastic continuity amid unresolved amnesty, fiscal, foreign, and military problems.

options.label: Receive the final memorial of the reign.
options.consequence: The record is sealed for the next emperor. Ferdinand's victories remain real; so do the wars they did not end.

options.label: Order a final settlement summary for Ferdinand III.
options.consequence: The clerks gather the unsettled questions into one inheritance: authority, confession, debt, armies, and peace.
